beats.narration_text: Ciao, this is Liam, in for Bear. Jow-hway Lee's Dusk Duel is a 2D fighting game, and assignment seven adds two animation clips: a lantern flame that loops on the background, and an arc that sweeps beside every kick and commits. Jow-hway chose the clips, the routes and the frame counts, and judged every strip. Claude Code built the clips, the scenes and the tests.

beats.narration_text: Here's the running game: a Movie Maker capture of an isolated copy, with scripted input. On the title screen, both lanterns already burn. That's clip one, a sprite sheet flipped frame by frame, and it loops. Then the round starts, Ah-kah-ken walks in and kicks, and the pale arc beside the leg is clip two, a cutout rig. It plays once per kick, and commits.

beats.narration_text: In the brief, these are Jow-hway's choices. The lantern flame is a cycle: a Sprite 2D with an animation player frame track, set to loop. The kick arc is a committing action: two polygons on a pivot, keyed as resource text, with no loop. Each animated property has one authority, and each clip has its own clock.

beats.narration_text: The sheet comes first. Jow-hway chose to generate it by code, and Claude Code wrote the generator, so there's no downloaded art, and the licence is the repository's MIT. Forty-eight by thirty-two pixels: four columns and two rows of twelve by sixteen cells. Cell n is frame n. Every flame's base sits on the same pixel, six, fifteen, so the sprite is offset by minus six, minus fifteen, and the flame stands still.

beats.narration_text: Here's the frame track that reads it. Line eleven: the track writes the sprite's frame. Line fifteen: eight keys, a tenth of a second apart, ten frames a second, matching the step on line seven. Line eighteen: cells zero to seven, in order. Line seventeen: update one, discrete, so the frame jumps from cell to cell. Line five, length point eight: one more interval after the last key, so seven wraps straight to zero. And line six turns the loop on.

beats.narration_text: Question one: what is a clip? Not a movie. A list of tracks, each a node path, a property, and keys at times. Nothing checks that path while the clip plays. Mutation one removed a single letter from the rotation track's property. The log shows no engine error at all: the arc would simply never turn. Only the read-back, which asks every track to resolve, failed. Claude Code met the same silence too, in its own probe: a track that moved nothing and printed nothing.

beats.narration_text: Question four: designing feel in frames. The constants in the code say seven, then five, then sixteen. But the tick a kick starts is frame zero, and the hit check runs only while frame is above seven and at most twelve. Counted from the code: startup, eight frames; active, five; recovery, fifteen; idle on frame twenty-eight. Jow-hway chose the measured counts. Divide by sixty, and the keys go at zero, zero point one three three three, zero point two one six seven, and zero point four six six seven seconds, the clip's length.

beats.narration_text: Those keys, as text. Line thirty-five: seven key times, on every phase boundary and the frame before it. Line thirty-eight: the pivot's angle, wound back to a hundred degrees during startup, then sweeping down to minus fifteen at the hitbox. Line thirty-six, the spacing: a transition of two accelerates into the active frames, and point four settles through recovery. Line forty-three: a second track fades the arc in and out.

beats.narration_text: And the committed strip, a fixture capture at thirty frames a second, two ticks per frame. Frame ten, startup begins: a faint wind-up. Thirteen, wound back. Fourteen, active opens at full strength. Sixteen, the last active frame, its head on the foot. Seventeen, recovery, fading. Twenty-three, nearly gone. Twenty-four, idle: no arc.

beats.narration_text: That faint arc on frame ten is revision r one. In r zero it wasn't there: the fade began at alpha zero. That was Claude's reading. Jow-hway's own first look said just right, and the first verdict was nothing to change. Then Jow-hway asked for Claude's points to be fixed, and approved one change: alpha zero to point two five. Claude predicted that only the first frames would change, and the strip agreed. Jow-hway's verdict after play: it can be seen, just right.

beats.narration_text: Now, who moves the arc? Kick rig dot gd, on every physics tick, after Main has stepped the fighters and checked hits. Line thirty-two: if the state is kick, line thirty-five seeks the clip to the fighter's own frame over sixty. Any other state, line thirty-seven plays rest, and the arc is hidden. The player itself is on manual, so it never moves on its own.

beats.narration_text: Question two: one authority. Every animated property has exactly one writer. The lantern's frame: only its own animation player; its script just calls play and seek, once. The arc: the rig's player. The fighter's sprite already has a writer, fighter dot gd, every step. If a clip keyed that sprite too, the two would overwrite each other every tick, and the last write would win. The read-back checks that no track touches it. This film argues that from the code; no two-writer run was staged.

show.event: writers table and the two-writer case; Lantern card lights

props.title: One Authority
props.source: Source: godot/fighter/fighter.gd:286-291; godot/fighter/kick_rig.gd:1-11; godot/animations/lantern_flame.gd; logs/test_kick_readback_60fps.log:10-17; CHANGE-BRIEF predicted failure 4

beats.narration_text: Question three: the two clocks. The lanterns advance on the idle tick and read nothing from the game, which is why they burned through the pause. The arc never advances by itself: it's placed on the physics tick, the same tick where the hit check reads the active window. Measured across a whole kick, the largest gap between clip time and the fighter's frame over sixty: zero seconds.

beats.narration_text: What did the tests prove? The lantern read-back, forty-seven checks: slicing, discrete keys a tenth apart, the loop, and a clean seam. The kick read-back, fifty-two: keys on every boundary, a sixtieth step, no loop, and no track on the fighter's sprite. States, fifty-eight; edges, thirty-eight; and the nineteen behaviour pins held before and after. Three mutations failed them. The fourth, an empty import cache, couldn't fail: neither clip is imported.

show.event: suites and mutations; Read-backs card lights

props.title: What The Tests Proved
props.source: Source: TEST-REPORT.md (A7); logs/test_lantern_readback_60fps.log:51, test_kick_readback:56, test_anim_states, test_kick_edges, test_pins_a7:44; logs/mutation_a7_1..4

beats.narration_text: What no headless run can show is the look. Those were Jow-hway's checks in the running game. The seam, over five wraps: no stutter. The kick: the phases can be told apart, and after an interrupt, the arc disappears. The flame: same place, no drift. On dark and lantern-lit stone: clearly visible. Recorded as given; Claude Code did not watch.

beats.narration_text: The agent made mistakes, and checks caught them. It guessed the jump lasts forty-four ticks; the pin said forty-two. Its lanterns broke an assignment six draw-order test. It wrote that input returns on kick frame twenty-eight; the edge test found twenty-nine. A probe track moved nothing. Four harness bugs, and two failed sign-ins. Finally, Claude's strip reading guessed that a thin line was an edge between polygons; its own renders showed it was the old whiff streak.

beats.narration_text: Verdict. Checked: both clips read back, every state plays the right clip, the arc freezes in hitstop and pause, vanishes on an interrupt, and sits zero seconds from the hit check. Uncertain: the left lantern is hidden at the start position; the empty-cache mutation cannot fail; the interrupt tests inject their hits; and revision r one came from Claude's reading, approved and judged by Jow-hway. Jow-hway chose the clips, routes, counts and clocks, wrote the answers, ran the strips and judged them. Claude Code built the rest. The sheet is generated by code, under MIT. Next step: a mutation that keys the fighter's sprite, to watch two authorities fight.
